name: Compute Hardware
oneLiner: The chips that do the maths: GPUs and other accelerators, their fast memory, and the links between them.

analogy.text: A kitchen: chips are the cooks, memory is the counter space, and interconnect is how fast cooks can pass dishes to each other.
analogy.breaks: Cooks work independently. Thousands of accelerators must act as one machine in lockstep, so the network between them matters as much as the chips.

examples: Low-precision formats such as BF16, FP8 and FP4
NVLink-style links and open standards such as UALink
Home hardware: consumer RTX cards, DGX Spark, Apple silicon
givesAbove: Raw arithmetic throughput and memory, exposed to software through platforms such as CUDA or ROCm.
needsBelow: Power, cooling and fabricated silicon from Physical & Energy.

walkthrough.title: A home user wants a 70B model
walkthrough.text: Someone wants to run a 70-billion-parameter open model at home. The work is billions of multiplications per token, which is what a GPU's thousands of cores are for.

walkthrough.title: Fewer bits per number
walkthrough.text: At 16 bits the weights need about 140 GB. Stored at 4 bits they need about 35 GB, and the chip moves and multiplies far more numbers per second.

walkthrough.title: Fit first, then speed
walkthrough.text: 35 GB won't fit in one consumer card's memory. Once it fits somewhere, every token re-reads those weights, so memory bandwidth sets the tokens per second.

walkthrough.title: Two cards, one link
walkthrough.text: Two cards split the layers between them and pass a small result across PCIe for each token. Splitting inside every layer would need a much faster link.

walkthrough.title: The same story at data-centre scale
walkthrough.text: Frontier models face the same limits, scaled up: low-precision formats, stacked HBM, and NVLink-style links that join many accelerators into the clusters of the layer above.
